A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HATReID-MOT work, with matching authors, core method, and substantial overlapping experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive restructuring.

before.justification: v1 reports original tracking experiments on DanceTrack, SportsMOT, MOT17, and TAO, including component ablations, feature visualizations, and inference speed.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds hybrid-tracker evaluations, MOT20 validation results, supervised-FLD comparisons, and quantitative feature-discriminability analyses.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains history-supervised FLD over recent features, temporally weighted trajectory centroids, and fusion of original and transformed similarities. The centroid component is renamed and historical labeling explained more explicitly. Hybrid experiments reuse this transformation without specifying a new HAT component or altered projection procedure.

E1.justification: The four original benchmarks remain. v2 adds MOT20 validation experiments for crowded pedestrian tracking in Appendix B.2 and Table 11, extending coverage within the existing pedestrian-tracking domain rather than introducing a different task.

E2.justification: v2 adds ByteTrack-ReID, OC-SORT-ReID, Hybrid-SORT-ReID, several end-to-end comparators, and training-set-supervised FLD. Comparator membership also contracts: Deep OC-SORT disappears from DanceTrack comparisons, although evaluated on MOT20, and StrongSORT disappears from MOT17. DiffusionTrack's DanceTrack comparison is retained in appendix Table 12.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include the worst-1000 similarity-margin diagnostic, a training-set-fitted FLD control, with/without-HAT hybrid-tracker comparisons, and shared-FastReID-weight MOT20 validation. Table 12 expands DanceTrack evaluation with localization and identity precision, recall, and error-count metrics. These additions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds discriminability-versus-association analyses, cross-dataset separability comparisons, and supervised-versus-history-aware FLD ablation in Table 9. It extends the fusion sweep to alpha = 0.4 and reports unsuccessful confidence-weighting and hard-trajectory-weighting attempts in Appendix D. The original component sweeps and qualitative separation evidence are largely retained.

E5.justification: Unlike v1, v2 reports regression statistics and shaded fit bands: Figure 2a gives R-squared = 0.630 and p = 2.17e-6; Figure 6a gives 0.296 and 0.000111. The bands' confidence level and construction are unspecified. Neither version reports repeated-run or seed uncertainty for benchmark tracking scores.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial hybrid, MOT20, supervised-FLD, diagnostic, and detailed-metric results. For example, HAT-OC-SORT-ReID achieves 81.2 HOTA on SportsMOT, and HAT-FastReID-MOT achieves 61.2 on MOT20 validation. The retained tuned, non-joint-training SportsMOT row changes from 79.3/72.1 to 78.9/71.3 HOTA/AssA. Many original scores remain, while some metric entries are removed.

T1.justification: v2 formally defines the positive-versus-hardest-negative similarity margin and its worst-1000 aggregation. It corrects the class-mean denominator from N in v1 Equation 6 to Nc in v2 Equation 5. However, the explicit multivariate trace criterion and eigenvector characterization are replaced by a less precise matrix quotient. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claim that sequence-conditioned, training-free feature transformation improves MOT remains. v2 extends the stated contributions to successful integration into hybrid trackers and associated state-of-the-art claims, beyond v1's emphasis on appearance-only trackers and zero-shot transfer. The underlying research objective is unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets limited MOT17 gains through already-separable appearances, supplements the MASA discussion with dependence on initial feature quality, and uses supervised FLD to argue for sequence-specific adaptation. Expanded limitations discuss motion-dominated hybrid pipelines, inability to directly modify end-to-end trackers, density-related computational costs, and omitted recent comparators.

D1.justification: v2 documents oracle confidence scores, explicit per-table ablation settings, and visualization sampling details, including 15-frame examples and 10 sequences with 40 frames each. It clarifies the timing boundary and reports baseline speed. The code link changes from HELLORPG to MCG-NJU; actual repository availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially around appearance customization, discussing adaptive affinity, trajectory long-tail handling, TOPIC, CATrack, and appearance purification. v2 explicitly distinguishes these approaches from sequence-specific feature-space adaptation and claims the first systematic explanation and practical solution. This goes beyond v1's broader tracking-paradigm survey.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 separates Preliminary from Method, introduces an explicit contribution list, reorganizes comparisons by tracker family, incorporates the former zero-shot section into broader comparisons, and substantially restructures the appendices with a new Discussions section.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting, with extensively reorganized tables and figures. v2 adds correlation and distribution plots, fitting-strategy and MOT20 tables, compact and detailed MOT17 presentations, and a rotated extended-metrics table. Existing pipeline and feature visualizations are reused or rearranged, and several tables have reduced metric columns.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrated gains but lacked a direct control testing history conditioning against globally fitted FLD and offered no hybrid-integration evidence. v2's Table 9, separability analyses, hybrid experiments, and MOT20 evaluation substantially strengthen explanatory support and demonstrated applicability. Added implementation details and limitations improve scrutiny. These gains outweigh local defects: the less precise Fisher objective and Section 5.3's claim to surpass SambaMOTR despite Table 1 reporting 66.9 versus 67.2 HOTA.
